extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and readers interested in mathematical logic and the foundations of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Conditions and key steps required to formulate and prove Gödel's incompleteness theorems for a formal axiomatic system, including the technical prerequisites (arithmetization, provability predicate, diagonalization) and the consistency/ω-consistency assumptions. Also covers variants and alternative proofs (Rosser, Berry's paradox) and the formalizability needed for the second incompleteness theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetization of syntax / Gödel numbering
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements in the system can be represented by natural numbers (Gödel numbers); every formula or statement that can be formulated in the system gets a unique number, and it is possible to mechanically convert back and forth between formulas and Gödel numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties of statements (such as provability) are translated into properties of their Gödel numbers so that questions about provability become arithmetical questions about numbers. Examples: encoding text via ASCII sequences; the system must be strong enough to support reasoning about numbers that represent formulae and statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and formalization of a provability predicate (Bew(y))
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a formula Bew(y) that, using arithmetical relations, states 'there exists a number x that is the Gödel number of a proof of the formula encoded by y' (i.e. 'y is provable').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bew(y) is an abbreviation for a long arithmetical formula; an important feature is that if a statement p is provable then Bew(G(p)) is also provable, because any proof of p has a corresponding Gödel number. The formal provability predicate must be definable inside the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagonalization / Diagonal lemma (construction of self-referential sentence)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any sufficiently strong formal system and any statement form F(x) there is a statement p such that the system proves p ↔ F(G(p)). By letting F be the negation of Bew(x), one obtains p ↔ ¬Bew(G(p)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a method to construct a sentence that (indirectly) asserts its own unprovability, avoiding infinite regress by using Gödel numbering. The lemma underlies the construction of the Gödel sentence; an illustrative English analogue is given in the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness / computability of the system
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal system must be effective (e.g., axioms/derivation rules are recursively enumerable / 'general recursive') so that syntactic relations (proof, formula) can be arithmetized and manipulated mechanically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The requirement that the system be effective is central to Gödel's theorem and later refinements (Rosser). It ensures proofs and checking can be represented by arithmetical relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Containment of elementary arithmetic (ability to represent arithmetic operations and recursive relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The system must be strong enough to support reasoning about numbers in general and to represent specific arithmetic facts and computable/arithmetical relations (typically 'elementary arithmetic' suffices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows the system to express relations about Gödel numbers and simulate the computations needed for the arithmetization of syntax; many formulations require the system to contain a fragment of arithmetic sufficient to represent recursive predicates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and ω-consistency assumptions (what is needed to derive undecidability)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show the constructed sentence p is not provable one needs only the assumption that the system is consistent; to show its negation is not provable (so p is undecidable) Gödel's original proof used the stronger assumption of ω-consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the system is ω-consistent, it proves neither p nor ¬p. If only consistent, the system may prove ¬p (giving a false provable sentence) and thus be not ω-consistent. Rosser's improvement replaces ω-consistency with simple consistency (see Rosser entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rosser's improvement (avoiding ω-consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rosser proved in 1936 that the hypothesis of ω-consistency in Gödel's original proof can be replaced by simple consistency by altering the Gödel sentence appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields the incompleteness theorem in its modern form: for any consistent, effectively axiomatizable theory containing enough arithmetic, there exists a sentence neither provable nor disprovable. The entry highlights historical development and the modern requirement of simple consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalizability of the first theorem within the system (requirements for the second incompleteness theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove the second incompleteness theorem one must formalize within the system S various facts about provability used in the proof of the first theorem using a formal predicate for provability; in particular the entire proof of the first theorem must be formalizable inside S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once the first theorem is formalizable in S (and the provability predicate satisfies the needed properties), one shows that if S could prove its own consistency then S would prove an unprovable sentence, yielding a contradiction. This is why the second theorem concludes S cannot prove Cons(S).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert–Bernays provability conditions / properties of the provability predicate
rubrics_metrics.description: Various facts about provability used in the proofs (for example, if T proves φ then T proves Bew(G(φ)), and Bew must behave appropriately under logical implication and modus ponens) must be expressible and provable inside the system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These formal properties (often called the Hilbert–Bernays provability conditions) are needed to carry the meta-argument into the object theory for the second incompleteness theorem and related results like Löb's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence of incompleteness under adding axioms (new undecidable sentences arise)
rubrics_metrics.description: If one adds p or ¬p as an axiom to avoid the incompleteness, the definition of 'being a Gödel number of a proof' changes (Bew changes), so applying the diagonal lemma to the new Bew yields a new sentence p' undecidable in the extended system (if it is ω-consistent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why 'adding missing axioms' does not remove the phenomenon: each consistent extension has its own Gödel sentence, so incompleteness recurs in the extended theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative proof methods (Berry's paradox / Boolos and Kripke variants)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are alternative proofs of the first incompleteness theorem using other paradoxical constructions (e.g., Berry's paradox) that construct true but unprovable sentences and give a different intuition for incompleteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boolos and others sketch such proofs; these approaches show different reasons for incompleteness and can emphasize computability/recursively enumerable set arguments rather than self-referential provability predicates.
